title: Same atoms, different shapes
question: How can two molecules built from the same atoms in the same sequence still differ?
hook: A drug can be hurt or helped by nothing more than which way its atoms point in space.
idea: Stereoisomers share a formula and bonded sequence but differ in how atoms sit in space, and that difference can matter in medicine.

beats.prompt: A drug comes as two enantiomers, but a patient is given only one of them. What does the body do?

choices.label: It produces the other enantiomer too
It keeps only the form that was given
choices.feedback: It sounds tidy, but in the body thalidomide undergoes racemization, so the other form appears anyway.

choices.label: It destroys the form that was given
choices.feedback: Nothing in the facts suggests the given form vanishes; the other form is made instead.

beats.explain: Thalidomide undergoes racemization, so even a single administered enantiomer leads to the other being produced by metabolism.

beats.prompt: match each way of drawing a bond to what it shows
pairs: Bond receding away from the viewer
Bond in the plane of the molecule
beats.explain: These simplified conventions show 3D positions of atoms around a stereocenter.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Only (S)-ibuprofen is active in reducing inflammation and pain.
So the (R) and (S) forms must act the same way in the body.
So a drug's spatial arrangement can matter for how it works.
beats.explain: Only the (S) form is active, so the two isomers do not act the same way.
